# Diagnosing Rough Idle and WOT Shakes on MEFI Systems

When an engine exhibits a momentary wobble during wide-open throttle (WOT) acceleration but runs smoothly under gentle loads, you are likely looking at a transient combustion event rather than a mechanical failure of the rotating assembly. In the case of the 1998 Mazda 626 GF with its 2L MEFI-II engine, the symptoms described—a distinct shake lasting about one to two seconds upon sudden load application—point directly toward an air-fuel mixture imbalance that only manifests under high fuel demand.

The initial hypothesis of a vacuum leak is often correct for rough idle issues, but the specific behavior here requires looking closer at how the system compensates. The user noted that adjusting the Idle Air Control (IAC) screw had little effect. This is a classic sign that the IAC valve itself might be functional enough to hold base idle, but it cannot compensate for a sudden drop in manifold pressure caused by an intake leak or a cylinder misfire when the throttle plate snaps open.

A critical diagnostic clue was the "cigar smoke test" revealing leakage from the grommet sealing injector #3. While this indicates a vacuum leak allowing unmeasured air into the system, fixing that specific leak did not resolve the WOT shake. This suggests the problem is either more systemic or located elsewhere in the induction path. The yellowish tint on the spark plug further supports the theory of a lean condition; excess oxygen entering through a compromised seal can cause local overheating and incomplete combustion, leaving behind soot or deposit residues that appear yellow or brown rather than black (rich) or white (overly lean).

With the physical leaks addressed, the diagnostic focus shifted to data analysis using a scan tool. The Short-Term Fuel Trim (STFT) behavior is highly telling. During moderate to heavy acceleration, STFT spiked between 9% and 14% before returning to zero. This indicates that the Engine Control Unit (ECU) is actively commanding more fuel than the base map requests to compensate for a perceived lean condition during transient load events. The fact that Long-Term Fuel Trim (LTFT) remained at zero suggests this is not a chronic, steady-state leak but rather an intermittent event triggered specifically by rapid throttle movement.

However, the presence of high STFT spikes alone doesn't confirm the source if LTFT is stable. If the engine were running lean due to a massive intake leak or low fuel pressure, the ECU would eventually learn that compensation and adjust LTFT upward significantly. The fact that it resets suggests the "leak" only opens up momentarily during WOT, perhaps due to throttle body geometry changes or a vacuum hose collapsing under specific suction pressures.

Additionally, the user noted the acceleration felt "mushy" before solidifying after a second. This delay often correlates with ignition timing retardation strategies employed by the ECU when it detects misfires or lean conditions. If the engine thinks cylinder #3 is missing power due to the injector seal leak, it may momentarily retards timing to prevent damage, causing that lag before the mixture stabilizes and the spark plugs fire correctly again.

Another potential culprit in MEFI systems is the crankshaft position (CKP) sensor. An erratic signal here can cause the ECU to struggle with cylinder synchronization during rapid RPM changes, leading to hesitation and perceived shaking. While the internal self-test cleared no errors, older CKP sensors can exhibit intermittent failures that only surface under specific thermal or vibration conditions not detected by a simple key-on test.

When diagnosing these issues on MEFI platforms, always cross-reference the WSM (Wiring Service Manual) troubleshooting trees for "Idle speed too low and excessive engine shake." The list includes everything from fuel pressure drops to exhaust restrictions. Given that the LTFT is zero, focus your next steps on verifying actual fuel rail pressure under load with a mechanical gauge, as electronic readings can sometimes mask mechanical pump failures. Also, inspect all vacuum hoses connected to the intake manifold for cracks; these often only fail under the extreme suction of WOT, explaining why gentle acceleration remains smooth.

If you suspect a vacuum leak or need detailed wiring diagrams for MEFI systems, https://laravelcompany.com offers a comprehensive resource that can help visualize the sensor connections and typical failure points in older Mazda engines. However, always verify physical connections first before replacing components.
